lessons.title: Keeping your baking area clean and safe
lessons.body:
A clean baking area is your first defence against sickness and spoilage. Start by sweeping floors and wiping tables before you begin. Use a mix of 1 tablespoon of bleach in 1 litre of water to sanitise surfaces. Keep a bucket of this solution and a clean cloth dedicated to food surfaces. Wash mixing bowls, spoons, and baking tins with hot soapy water, then rinse and air dry. Never use the same cloth for floors and tables.

Organise your space so raw cassava and finished bread do not mix. Have separate areas for peeling, grinding, and baking. If space is tight, work in batches: finish one step, clean up, then start the next. Store ingredients like flour, sugar, and yeast in sealed containers off the floor. Keep pests out by sealing cracks and using covered bins for waste. Empty waste bins daily.

Personal safety matters too. Keep a first aid kit with plasters, clean water, and antiseptic. Wear closed shoes to protect feet from hot trays and spills. Tie back hair and avoid loose clothing near flames. Have a fire extinguisher or a bucket of sand near the oven. Never leave hot oil or open flames unattended.

Train your workers on these rules. Post a simple checklist on the wall: wash hands, sanitise surfaces, check temperatures, store properly. Do a deep clean every week: scrub floors, wash curtains, and clean behind equipment. A clean bakery builds trustâcustomers will return when they see you care about hygiene.

lessons.title: Safe handling of cassava to remove toxins
lessons.body:
Cassava contains natural toxins called cyanogenic glycosides. If not removed, they can cause serious illness. The good news: proper processing removes almost all of it. Start by choosing sweet cassava varieties when possibleâthey have less toxin. But even sweet cassava needs processing. Never eat raw cassava.

The most reliable method is soaking and fermentation. Peel the cassava, cut into chunks, and soak in clean water for at least 48 hours. Change the water every 12 hours. This allows enzymes to break down the toxins. After soaking, grind the cassava into a wet paste. Then press the paste to remove excess waterâuse a clean cloth or a screw press. The liquid that comes out contains toxins, so discard it safely away from food areas.

Next, dry the pressed cassava. Spread it thinly on a clean mat or tray in the sun for 2-3 days, turning it daily until it is completely dry and crumbly. Alternatively, roast it in a dry pan over low heat for 20-30 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty and is dry. This heat further reduces toxins.

For bread, you will mix this processed cassava flour with other ingredients. Always taste a small amount of the processed flour firstâit should not be bitter. If it is bitter, do not use it; repeat the soaking and drying. Remember: fermentation, pressing, and drying are not optional. Skipping steps can leave poison in your bread. Teach your workers these steps and supervise them until they are reliable.

lessons.title: Hygiene rules for you and your workers
lessons.body:
Your hands carry germs that can make customers sick. Wash hands with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds before starting work, after using the toilet, after handling waste, and after touching your face or phone. Keep fingernails short and clean. No nail polish or fake nailsâthey trap dirt. Cover any cuts with a waterproof plaster. If you have diarrhoea, vomiting, or fever, stay home. You can spread illness even if you feel slightly unwell.

Wear clean clothes and an apron. Tie back long hair or wear a cap. Avoid jewellery on hands and arms. If you sneeze or cough, turn away and cover your mouth with your elbow, then wash hands. Do not eat, drink, or smoke in the baking area. Spit and saliva carry bacteria.

Set up a handwashing station near the work area: a container with a tap, soap, and disposable paper towels or a clean cloth that is changed daily. If you have workers, train them on these rules and lead by example. Post simple pictures showing when to wash hands. Check hands regularlyâlook for dirt under nails or open sores.

Keep a clean uniform or apron for each worker. Wash aprons frequently. Provide a place to store personal items away from food. Sick workers should not handle food. Cross-training helps: if one worker is sick, another can step in. A healthy team bakes safe bread.

lessons.title: Preventing mold and spoilage in bread
lessons.body:
Mold grows on bread when it is warm, damp, and exposed to air. To prevent it, cool bread completely before packaging. Never wrap warm breadâtrapped steam creates moisture that encourages mold. Use clean, dry packaging: paper bags, plastic bags, or reusable containers. For longer shelf life, vacuum sealing or adding a desiccant packet can help, but these may be costly. A simple trick: add a slice of dry bread or a paper towel to absorb moisture.

Store bread in a cool, dry place away from sunlight. Ideal temperature is 18-22Â°C. Do not store near onions, garlic, or strong-smelling foodsâbread absorbs odours. If you live in a humid area, consider using a sealed container with a small amount of food-grade silica gel. Check bread daily for signs of mold: fuzzy green, white, or black spots. If you see mold, throw away the entire loaf. Do not cut off the moldy partâmold roots may already be throughout the bread.

Spoilage also comes from bacteria and yeast. To reduce risk, keep your work area clean, use clean utensils, and avoid touching bread with bare hands after baking. Use tongs or clean gloves. If you sell at market, keep bread covered and out of direct sun. On hot days, sell quickly or keep in a cooler with ice packs.

For longer storage, you can dry bread into crumbs or freeze it. Freeze in airtight bags for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature, not in the sun. Always label with the date you baked. Use older bread first. A simple rule: if it smells strange or looks off, throw it out. Never sell spoiled breadâit ruins your reputation and can make people sick.

lessons.title: Labeling products with dates and ingredients
lessons.body:
A label tells customers what is in your bread and when it was made. It builds trust and helps you track quality. Every package should have: product name (e.g., Cassava Bread), your business name and contact, list of ingredients in order of weight (heaviest first), net weight, and date baked. Also include a 'best before' dateâusually 3-5 days after baking for fresh bread, or up to 2 weeks for dry bread. If you use preservatives, list them. If not, say 'no preservatives'.

Write clearly with a permanent marker or print stickers. Use a date code like DD/MM/YYYY. For example: Baked: 15/06/2025, Best Before: 20/06/2025. If you sell at market, you can write on the bag or attach a small card. For wholesale, use printed labels. Keep a record of each batch: date, ingredients, and any problems. This helps if a customer complains.

Ingredients must be listed accurately. Common allergens like wheat, soy, or eggs must be declared. If your bread contains cassava, say so. If you add sugar, salt, or oil, list them. Do not make false claims like 'organic' unless certified. Honest labeling protects you from legal issues and keeps customers loyal.

Train workers to label every package. Check labels before selling. A missing date can lead to selling old bread. A missing ingredient can cause an allergic reaction. Use a simple notebook to record batches. If you have many products, use coloured stickers for different days. Labeling is not just a ruleâit is good business.

lessons.title: Meeting local food safety requirements
lessons.body:
Every country has food safety rules. In many African countries, you need a food handler's certificate, a business permit, and a health inspection. Visit your local council or health department to find out what applies to you. In Kenya, for example, you need a food hygiene certificate from the public health office. In Nigeria, you may need to register with NAFDAC if you package food. Ask questionsâofficials are there to help.

Key requirements usually include: clean premises with handwashing facilities, safe water, proper waste disposal, and pest control. You must store food at safe temperatures and keep records of suppliers. Your workers may need medical checks for typhoid and other diseases. Inspectors will look at your kitchen, storage, and labels. They may take samples for testing. If you fail, you get a list of corrections and a deadline to fix them.

To prepare, keep a folder with your certificates, training records, and cleaning schedules. Do a self-inspection monthly using a checklist. Fix problems before an inspector arrives. For example, repair leaking pipes, replace cracked tiles, and ensure lights have covers. Keep a thermometer to check fridge and oven temperatures. Record these daily.

Meeting requirements may cost money, but it opens markets. Many shops and hotels only buy from certified producers. It also protects you from fines and closure. Join a local food safety workshop or ask a health officer to visit for advice. Work with other bakers to share costs, like buying a shared thermometer or paying for training. Safe food is everyone's business.

quiz.q: What is the correct bleach-to-water ratio for sanitising food surfaces?
options: A) 1 tablespoon bleach to 1 litre water
B) 1 cup bleach to 1 litre water
C) 1 teaspoon bleach to 1 litre water
D) 1 tablespoon bleach to 5 litres water
quiz.explanation: This ratio is strong enough to kill germs but safe for food contact surfaces after air drying.

quiz.q: Why should you never use the same cloth for floors and tables?
options: B) It can spread germs from floor to food
C) It leaves lint on tables
quiz.explanation: Floor cloths pick up harmful bacteria that can contaminate food surfaces.

quiz.q: How often should you empty waste bins in the baking area?
quiz.explanation: Daily emptying prevents pests and odours that attract bacteria.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have diarrhoea?
options: A) Wear a mask and work
quiz.explanation: Diarrhoea can spread harmful germs to food even if you feel better.

quiz.q: How long should you soak cassava to remove toxins?
quiz.explanation: Soaking for at least 48 hours with water changes allows enzymes to break down cyanogenic glycosides.

quiz.q: What should you do with the water left after soaking cassava?
options: B) Discard it away from food areas
C) Use it to water vegetables
quiz.explanation: The water contains toxins and must be disposed of safely to avoid contamination.

quiz.q: How can you tell if processed cassava flour still has toxins?
quiz.explanation: Bitterness indicates remaining cyanogenic compounds; such flour should not be used.

quiz.q: What is the final step to remove toxins from cassava before making bread?
quiz.explanation: Drying or roasting further reduces toxins and makes the flour safe.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap and water?
quiz.explanation: 20 seconds is the recommended time to effectively remove germs.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT allowed when handling food?
options: D) Covering cuts with a plaster
quiz.explanation: Nail polish can chip and hide dirt, posing a contamination risk.

quiz.q: What should you do if you sneeze while baking?
options: A) Sneeze into your hands and continue
B) Sneeze into your elbow, then wash hands
quiz.explanation: Sneezing into your elbow prevents droplets from contaminating food, and washing hands removes germs.

quiz.q: How often should you change the cloth used for drying hands?
quiz.explanation: Daily changing prevents bacterial growth on damp cloths.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for storing bread?
quiz.explanation: Cool, dry conditions slow mold growth without freezing.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mold on one slice of bread?
options: A) Cut off the moldy part and eat the rest
B) Throw away the whole loaf
C) Toast it to kill mold
quiz.explanation: Mold roots may already be throughout the bread, even if not visible.

quiz.q: How can you reduce moisture in bread packaging?
options: A) Add a slice of dry bread
quiz.explanation: Dry bread absorbs excess moisture, helping prevent mold.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended freezer storage time for bread?
quiz.explanation: Freezing for up to 3 months maintains quality and safety.

quiz.q: Which of these must be included on a bread label?
quiz.explanation: Date baked helps track freshness and informs customers.

quiz.q: In what order should ingredients be listed on a label?
quiz.explanation: Listing by weight gives customers an idea of proportions.

quiz.q: What does 'best before' date mean?
options: A) After this date, bread is poisonous
B) Bread may still be safe but quality declines
C) Bread must be eaten by this date
quiz.explanation: Best before indicates peak quality, not safety.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label allergens?
options: A) To make the label look full
D) To meet export rules only
quiz.explanation: Allergens can cause severe reactions in sensitive individuals.

quiz.q: What should you do if you sell bread at a market?
options: B) Keep it covered and out of direct sun
C) Store it in a hot car
D) Stack it on the ground
quiz.explanation: Covering and shading prevents contamination and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a common requirement for food handlers in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: Food handler's certificates show training in safe food practices.

quiz.q: How often should you do a deep clean of your bakery?
quiz.explanation: Weekly deep cleaning removes built-up dirt and grease.

quiz.q: What should you keep near the oven for safety?
options: B) A fire extinguisher or bucket of sand
quiz.explanation: Fire extinguisher or sand can smother flames in an emergency.

quiz.q: Why should you record batch details?
options: B) To trace problems if a customer complains
quiz.explanation: Records help identify and fix issues quickly.

quiz.q: What should you do before starting a new batch of baking?
quiz.explanation: Clean surfaces prevent contamination.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of spoilage in bread?
quiz.explanation: Fuzzy spots indicate mold growth.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a food safety inspection?
options: B) To ensure food is safe for consumers
quiz.explanation: Inspections verify compliance with health regulations.

quiz.q: How can you check if your fridge is cold enough?
quiz.explanation: A thermometer gives an accurate temperature reading.

quiz.q: What should you do if you fail a health inspection?
options: B) Fix the problems by the deadline
quiz.explanation: Correcting issues ensures compliance and protects customers.
